meta.title: An Analysis of Information Security Vulnerabilities in the Sussex Police 101 Non‑Emergency Call Handling System
meta.source_file_name: An Analysis of Information Security Vulnerabilities in the Sussex Police 101 Non-Emergency Call Handling System.pdf
meta.source_path: /mnt/data/An Analysis of Information Security Vulnerabilities in the Sussex Police 101 Non-Emergency Call Handling System.pdf

executive_summary: Two separate 101 interactions revealed personal data (OIC’s name) by bypassing standard security via (1) strategic confusion and (2) social‑engineering.
Primary weaknesses are human/procedural rather than technical: service‑vs‑security goal conflict, exploitation of Victims’ Code framing, and handler susceptibility under cognitive load.
A determined caller can circumvent formal disclosure channels (e.g., SAR) due to frontline discretion and process gaps.

findings.finding: Handlers prioritised resolving the caller’s stated problem over strict data‑security rules.
Victim‑rights framing created psychological barriers to refusal and drove discretion.
findings.evidence_excerpt_ref: Report executive summary (Exploitation of Victim Status)

findings.finding: Switching between similar case records increased cognitive load, leading to disclosure.
Narrative of neglect + invoking Veritas + emotional disclosure overcame protocol.

tactics_documented.name: Strategic Confusion
tactics_documented.goal: Create procedural uncertainty between two similar crime refs; obtain OIC name.

tactics_documented.name: Social Engineering
tactics_documented.goal: Leverage victim narrative, third‑party authority (Veritas), and emotional plea to obtain OIC name.

recommendations: Rebalance scripts to foreground security over service in disclosure scenarios; add mandatory stop‑phrases and escalation paths.
Harden verification when crime refs are presented: require multi‑factor knowledge checks beyond the number itself.
Add a ‘confusion protocol’: when multiple similar records exist, forbid personnel disclosure; require written follow‑up by OIC.
Train for social‑engineering red flags (third‑party authority invocation, emotional pressure) with role‑play drills.
Route personal‑data disclosures to formal processes (e.g., SAR), with logged reasons when exceptions occur.
